utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I deal with two matters, please? It relates to both Prosecution and Defence applications. The first is in respect of Mr. Sljivancanin's expert, Mr. Vuga. The Court will have received his report. I understand and may I say we have discussed this matter before coming into court, so I hope I accurately reflect what has been said and agreed. But that expert will be coming in, I believe, on Friday afternoon with a hope for him to give evidence, I believe, on the Monday. There may be a difficulty and it is as follows: Your Honour may remember when we presented the report of Mr. Pringle. Mr. Pringle's report had originally relied in some respects on witness statements, and in due course, he was then given transcripts of evidence and asked whether he considered his report had changed in any way at all as a result of the evidence as opposed to the witness statement. I understand that what is going to be done by the Defence is the same process, that they will show next weekend the witness statements -- sorry, the transcript of the witnesses who Mr. Vuga relies upon. The trouble, as I see it, is as follows: I suspect my learned friend will be asking the witness to look at the transcript, to ask whether it changes his report in any material particular. I don't know and neither does Mr. Lukic know whether that is going to be the case. But if I may deal with worst case scenario, it means really two things, firstly, that there will have to be an addendum to the report which we will receive probably on Monday, which will not give us enough time for our own expert to look at that report and to evaluate it for obviously the same day. So that is the first problem that I foresee. I don't know if it is possible for the transcripts to be sent to Mr. Vuga from today so that a supplementary report or addendum can be created and then we can proceed. But I am just concerned that with Mr. Vuga getting the report only at the weekend we will not have enough time to assess the weight of his report and whether it is changed in any significant way. So without any intention, we are, I believe, at risk of being substantially disadvantaged. So that is the first matter that I would wish to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You did say that you discussed this before the Chamber came in. Was there any sight of a solution?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I think there is a willing by Mr. Lukic to try to help. I don't deny that in any way, but for my part, I would have thought having dealt with this problem myself that the witness often needs a few days to look at the transcript and assess if it changes his report because, clearly, he may well be cross-examined on transcripts and on evidence, not just report. But my learned friend will be able to know the availability of the witness and what he will be able to do and what he wants to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You were moving to a second matter, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The second matter deals with Witness 002, and the diary of 002. The Court had initially asked me for 002 to be made available to give evidence on the 11th of December. We did that. Matters have moved a little quicker than perhaps we had anticipated, although it will be fairly close, and therefore, I have asked for 002 to be brought to the Court, I believe it is the 6th of December. The problem that we may have in relation to that is as follows: My learned friend has asked for the whole diary to be translated. Now, obviously, we have translated parts over and above that which we deemed relevant, but from what I understand is I believe it's something like 130 pages to be translated upon my learned friend's request. The translators or the translation section say they cannot do it. Firstly, it's too big a task but perhaps more importantly, they find it very difficult to decipher the writing. We've had this problem before, if Your Honour remembers, with Mr. Kypr, where sometimes individuals had a style that can vary. What I was suggesting to my learned friend was as follows -- or twofold. First, I have not mentioned to him but I mention now. If in actual fact there are any parts that he wants to have translated and he himself, Mr. Borovic, believes that he can interpret it, would he be kind enough to give us what he believes to be the translation of that part. We will ask for the interpretation section to look at it and we will ask 002 to confirm whether that is correct. That is one option. The second option is as follows: That 002 is brought in on the 6th, as we hope we can now do, that he then sits down with a translator or an interpreter and goes through the parts that my learned friend wishes to have interpreted, and then we can have an agreed transcript of what that witness believes to be the accurate record of what he said. In my submission, that is the better option because it will be on the basis of his interpretation of the document, and therefore my learned friend would be in a position to cross-examine in the following way, isn't it right you came on Wednesday, you sat with some interpreters, you went through and you agreed this was what was said? And therefore, there is a validity in the cross-examination. So I just ask for the Court's guidance in relation to this. For my part, I would submit that the second option is the better and more accurate option and will not affect the overall timetable because the witness will still be able to give evidence on Monday, the 11th as you had originally requested. Those are the two matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, thank you, but the Chamber had been driven to the 11th by the prospect that Mr. Lukic would not finish his case until Friday, the 8th. The signs at present are that he will finish his case probably on the 6th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I would think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Because of that, it may even be earlier, but because of that, we have moved forward the timetable for P002 to give his further evidence, to the Thursday and Friday, the 5th and 6th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You are now contemplating a procedure that would extend him into the following week which we understood from counsel was not terribly convenient. It certainly makes it difficult for me to finish some other matters and hearings that I am trying to fit into that last week.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So the question that arises is whether you see it as possible for 002 to come even earlier in that week, earlier than Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I can certainly ask for that to be done. The other option of course is this: That he is called, my learned friends have got copies of the diary. He can be called, perhaps not on the 6th, but on the 7th, or if he's here I can get him a day earlier on the 6th, and there is cross-examination of him on the document. The only problem that I foresee as a practical problem and that is that my learned friend -- I mean it in the nicest possible way of saying, it doesn't say that, it says this and the witness says, no, it doesn't say that, it says this. And one is left with an impasse and I would have thought that the situation not resolved. For my part, I thought it was better that one looked at the areas that my learned friend wants to cross-examine on, get the witness to say what it is that section reports, have that transcribed and then my learned friend could cross-examine on an agreed translation. But I will certainly do what Your Honour wishes and try and bring him in earlier again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for that. The difficulty with the option you offer as a solution is you don't take account of the possibility of Mr. Lukic not agreeing with the witness's understanding of his own diary. An impasse may well result. That is something which this Chamber has become accustomed to in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I think unusually it's not Mr. Lukic who is contesting the diary. I think it's Mr. Borovic who will be dealing with the problem. I think -- it's Mr. Lukic as well. My apologies. I should have known.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moore. Now, Mr. Lukic, first the expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would only like to make comments in relation to the expert because the diary is something that I leave to Mr. Borovic, not because I'm any less interested, but because I have enough on my plate, that is our team has, concerning some other issues. As for the expert, I think it might be helpful to reach some sort of a clear cut solution. I talked to Mr. Moore this morning about that. I undertook firstly that Mr. Vuga would be in The Hague as soon as Thursday, probably Thursday afternoon, but we will be able to work with him, to proof him on Friday, Saturday and Sunday, given that Mr. Susnjar testifies on Friday. Mr. Bulatovic and I have distributed tasks among ourselves and I'll be able to start work with Mr. Vuga straight away. My assumption is there will be very few changes to his report, very few things that are new. I wish to show him a number of transcripts but only both of relevant testimonies that have any bearing on his report. As for any new exhibits that he's not aware of, I think there are a mere handful, since he was already familiar with most of the exhibits at the time he drafted his report, including those we exhibited through Mr. Sljivancanin. There are maybe five or six new exhibits that might have any bearing at all on his report. It is a technical impossibility for him to familiarise himself with the transcripts. He speaks German but he does not speak English. I don't think it's possible for anyone from our team to walk him through it. That would be very difficult. One thing that I can promise, and undertake on behalf of our team, is that by 10.00 on Monday, if there is any information to suggest that amendments should be made to his report, we will do it by 10.00 Monday in a written form. If everything goes to schedule, he should start testifying on Tuesday, in all likelihood. In the expectation that there will be few changes if any to his report, I think that should provide more than sufficient time for everyone else to examine him that Tuesday and Wednesday. What might require an additional effort on the part of the Registry is this. I see that we are scheduled for the morning of the 5th of December, whereas at half past 5 p.m., I see a status conference scheduled in this courtroom in another case. If we could switch things around there too so Mr. Vuga could perhaps start on the afternoon of the 5th that should be sufficient time, provided we submit any changes by Monday morning, that should provide sufficient time for everybody else to prepare for their examination of Mr. Vuga. At any rate, I think we will not be requiring more than a single session for the examination-in-chief of Mr. Vuga, possibly even less, which means that the other parties will have the remaining part of Tuesday and that Wednesday to cross-examine him. And then we have the 7th and the 8th of December freed up in this way, to do whatever it takes in relation to Witness 002. If Mr. Susnjar finishes early on Monday, or perhaps even as early as Friday, then we might want to not sit on Monday and then, if Tuesday afternoon is possible, I think everybody would be happy with that and two days with Mr. Vuga would be perfectly sufficient. One thing I can say right is with a high degree of certainty that there will be very few changes, if any, to his report. Maybe a handful of transcripts of certain witnesses that I'll be telling him about as you may be able to assume, these are our Defence witnesses that he perhaps was not familiar with at the time he produced his report. I think that would be a proposition by our Defence that is more than understandable. Of course, it is always up to the Chamber to rule on the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, can I say first that I would anticipate it will not be practical to change from an afternoon to a morning or a morning to an afternoon. A listing of that nature late in the day indicates to me that there has been a need to find that time when either counsel or Judges are available because of their involvement in some other case in the Tribunal. It's an unusual hour for a conference. So that I suspect you will find that either counsel or Judges or perhaps both are engaged and aren't available before that time. Of course, if it should be available, this Chamber is happy to move to the afternoon. But you must plan, I think, on the basis that it will be in the morning. Second, if the witness is arriving perhaps on Thursday, the question arises whether it might be possible to give notice at least orally earlier than Monday morning at 10.00, so that there is a more opportunity for Mr. Moore and his team to look at the nature of the changes. I appreciate it may be impractical to think of written notice before 10.00 a.m. on Monday, but oral notice may perhaps be possible by Saturday evening. May even be by Friday. So if you could keep that in mind. Thank you. The expert is clearly going to challenge both sides to ensure that the witness and his evidence, the evidence of the witness, is able to proceed with reasonable efficiency. And given the circumstances, the expected arrival of the witness on Thursday, it ought to be possible for some adequate notice, at least orally, to reach Mr. Moore in time to enable the preparation for the evidence which is expected to commence on Tuesday of the following week, with full written notice on the Monday morning by 10.00 a.m. So I think if we can have goodwill on both sides there, the expert situation may be able to resolve itself. We turn now to Mr. Borovic and P002.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I think there is no problem about that at all. The note in relation to P002 was scanned in a single day and it's already part of the system, which is ahead of the deadline that was imposed on us. As for the translation, it's not 132 pages, there are certain pages that only contain a single sentence. I think the total number of pages involved in that particular translation would not be beyond 10 pages. I move that P002 be called on the 4th of December, which is a Monday, and as Mr. Moore proposed, the witness, my own associate, who is a translator, and I can deal with the whole thing, which means that we can submit that translation or revisions very soon to the OTP and we can start on Wednesday which should be easy enough. It should be very easy to organise this new and amended schedule. It should be easy enough to deal with if the Prosecutor intends to call the witness on the 4th or on the 5th, Monday or Tuesday. It only takes one day for our own operation, that is interpreting the meaning of the words written down by him. He can just read them out, we can make a transcript and translate the whole thing. Even I was able to deciphers as many as 90 per cent of the words in that note because there is actually very little text. We followed the guidelines of the Chamber and we only had certain paragraphs translated. Two-thirds are in relation to things outside Vukovar that wasn't translated and that wasn't scanned. The scanning was only done because the Registry insisted that we should be able to inspect the whole document. So the OTP agrees we can be two days early with this witness. With my own assistant and with a translator, we can deal with this in a single day. I guarantee that. It's maybe one or two lines a page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Borovic. We would, I think, add to what you're contemplating. Firstly, of course, what is in mind is that the witness would actually give evidence on Thursday or Friday. That is the 7th or the 8th of December. He will be recalled then when Mr. Lukic's case is finished. Mr. Moore has indicated he will look into the possibility of the witness arriving earlier than Wednesday the 6th, to facilitate the witness looking at the diary. Another thing that appears would greatly facilitate the whole process for everybody would be that if you and Mr. Lukic were able to identify those pages or parts of pages which are of interest to you, instead of dealing with the whole of the diary, as you indicate, about two-thirds of which are of no relevance to this case whatsoever. If we know just what are the parts that are of interest to you and Mr. Lukic, that would greatly speed up what has to be done by Mr. Moore and what might need some interpretation. So could we ask you and Mr. Lukic, by the end of this week, to identify those parts of the diary? I would think it need only be a copy of what has been photographed now, with a marking on the side of any paragraphs that are of interest to you, and that would be enough, provided to Mr. Moore to enable him then to have the witness concentrate on those parts. Are those suggestions satisfactory to you, Mr. Moore?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, there is no problems about that. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We will better get the witness in before it's time to go home. Oh, Mr. Domazet, you're lost to my sight there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. The matter is I've just stood up. There is an issue that I wish to raise. It will seem now that I discussed this with Mr. Lukic, but it really has nothing to do with his proposal for Tuesday. It's this that I want to discuss. I received permission from the Court or information that the appeal in the Blagojevic case that I was in charge of would be dealt with the middle of the following week. Blagojevic is scheduled for Tuesday, 8 to 12.30 and Wednesday, 8 to 12. There is no co-counsel, so I have sole responsibility for that hearing. The problem is we have Tuesday and Wednesday, the morning sessions, for this case, and as far as I can tell, it's probably going to be Witness Vuga and I'm preparing for that witness because Mr. Vasic will be examining two other very important witnesses that same week. Any changes now in terms of me leaving Mr. Vasic to do something that I had been preparing, given the fact that he already has two very important witnesses, would be an uphill struggle for our Defence team. I am prepared of course to examine expert Witness Vuga and to do the Blagojevic-Jokic appeal, but one thing I would like to ask is this, one thing I was going to propose. What Mr. Lukic said: If possible to sit on Tuesday afternoon and Wednesday too, if possible, although, personally, I think if Mr. Lukic finishes the witness in a single session, I would probably not be taking more than the following one and a half or two sessions and would be wrapping up Witness Vuga on Tuesday. Tuesday would be important if there is no option for Wednesday afternoon because I would need to be in Courtroom I for the Blagojevic appeal. Therefore, if in any way possible, there was only the half hour for the Status Conference in the Limaj case that Tuesday, if that can be moved or perhaps held in another courtroom, that would be very helpful because I think Courtroom I happens to be not taken at the time. But that's nothing for me to look into, needless to say. That's my proposal. The situation I'm facing is extremely unpleasant. I was not consulted by the Court about these dates. I was simply told that this would be taking place the following week, and it was not within my power to change anything about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, the Court is going to enquire into the possibility whether there could be a move to the afternoon, not only because of what you say, but already because of what Mr. Lukic had said. The prospect, though, is still there that it will have to remain as it is. Now, that may mean that you will need to alter the order in which you deal with the witness to allow perhaps Mr. Borovic to go before you or in some other way to accommodate the situation. As soon as we know whether there can be a change in our listing from morning to afternoon, you will be contacted and Mr. Lukic and all counsel so that you will know what it is that lies ahead and how to plan your time. It's going to be tight that week and next. One of the Judges of this Chamber has to sit in another appeal, so there are difficulties at every point. The problem is we have three courtrooms, we have many more trials and appeals as well. So we will do what we can to assist. At the moment, I don't think we can do more to help than to see whether we can change the time of sitting. We will do that. Thank you. The next witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Would you please read allowed the affirmation on the card given to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please sit down. Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: And to you, Mr. Karanfilov.

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I will ask you now -- we have already discussed this, as we prepared you for the testimony, to wait for me to finish my question and then to start your answer for the sake of the transcript. Did you understand me?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karanfilov, I will now ask you for some details from your CV and could you please confirm that they are correct. First of all, can you please state your full name for the record?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Borce Karanfilov.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: When and where were you born?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: 22nd of April 1963, in Kocani, Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that from 1977 to 1981 you attended the military high school?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: From 1981 until 1985, you attended the military academy, the infantry department?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You began your service in the JNA in 1985 as a platoon commander in the Guards Brigade?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: In 1989, you were appointed the desk officer for the security matters in the Guards Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: In 1992, you received your new appointment in the security department of the Secretariat of the Defence?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Yes, the security department in the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: And where have you been since 2004?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: In 2004, I became the head of a --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: As regards your rank, what rank do you hold?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: I am a colonel of the Serbian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karanfilov, could you please wait for me to finish my question and then you begin your answer and could you please repeat your answer as to your posts since 2004?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: I'm the chief of the section for securing persons and facilities in the army and Ministry of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karanfilov, now let us address the events that are the focus of our attention here, the events in Vukovar. What I would like to know is whether in 1991, you were in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can you recall your post in 1991?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: I was the officer -- I was an officer in the security department in the Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Who was the chief of security in the Guards Brigade at that time?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: It was Mr. Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain to us here what were your tasks as the officer in the security organ?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: The security officer is in charge of counterintelligence, using the legal means to do so and legal equipment to do so. What does it mean? Using the proper equipment and methods of work, the security organ detects, documents and prevents enemy activities of foreign intelligent services, military intelligent services, aimed against the state and the law and order. The military prevents, detects and documents the enemy activities against the unit and within the unit itself. And also fights all kinds of criminal activities within his or -- his purview. So that would be the general idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karanfilov, could you please speak a little bit slower so that the interpreters can keep up? So among those tasks, were there any specific tasks that you had while you were in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please be more specific, what tasks?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: I was in charge of the functioning of the roadblocks in Negoslavci and the counter-intelligence protection of the rear command post of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: The rear command post of the brigade, where was it located, can you please tell us?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: It was located in the village of Berak and I was given this task because one of my colleagues was absent.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us where was the headquarters of the security organ?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: The security organs were located in the village of Negoslavci, in a private house.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: When we are talking about the security organ, can you please tell us how many people were there in the security organ?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Six in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please recall who were these people and what tasks, what duties, they had?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: It was Major Sljivancanin, as the chief. Major Vukasinovic as the deputy. Captain First Class Karan, assistant for counter-intelligence. Mr. Borisavljevic, myself, and warrant officer Momcilovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karanfilov, one date that is quite undisputed here is the 18th of November, the day of the liberation or the occupation of Vukovar. Do you remember that date, the 18th of November? Do you remember any activities that you had on that date and what makes you still remember those activities?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: I don't remember the date. I have stated that several times now, and I only remember the activities that are still etched in my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What events make you remember those events, not the date, but the events -- what is the first event that is striking in your memory?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: The first event is the negotiations on the surrender of the Mitnica Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: As regards the surrender of the Mitnica Battalion, and we have already determined that it happened on the 18th, so I will not be trying to make you be more specific about the dates, but can you please tell me what were your activities related to the surrender of the Mitnica Battalion, who gave you those tasks and what kind of tasks did you have?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: My first task was given to me by Major Sljivancanin, to prepare a team for the direct, physical security of Colonel Pavkovic. And to take that team and to secure -- to provide security for Colonel Pavkovic during the negotiations at the site in this period. That's what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Could we please now clarify who is Colonel Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Colonel Pavkovic is a representative of the cabinet of the federal secretary of National Defence in Vukovar. He was in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: And when did you start performing this task?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: This task was received in the morning. The team was set up, and together with Colonel Pavkovic and the team, at around 10.00, approximately, we left Negoslavci and went to a small house where the negotiations were supposed to be held.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: And were negotiations in fact held?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Yes. There were negotiations. The representatives of the other side arrived after we had, and the negotiations of the two parties were held there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karanfilov, were you in the room where the negotiations were going on?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: No, not during the negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you to wait for my question to finish.

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: We were not there during the negotiations. We stood in front of the house until the negotiations ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember -- do you know who participated in the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: It was Mr. Pavkovic and the representative of the International Red Cross, if I'm not mistaken, and I don't know who was there representing the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember how long these negotiations lasted?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: I think that the negotiations lasted between an hour and a half and two hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: After the negotiations ended, Mr. Karanfilov, did you have any activities related to the so-called Mitnica Battalion?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: After the negotiations ended, I went back to Negoslavci with Colonel Pavkovic, and then I reported to Major Sljivancanin that I had been tasked by Colonel Pavkovic to head in an hour, hour and a half, to start the process of the surrender of some units and Colonel Pavkovic had already informed them that the negotiations had been successful and that within an hour to an hour and a half, the ZNG units would start to surrender.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Could you specify the time when the surrender started and who was present there, if you remember? Were you there? Was there anyone else there with you?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: It was in the afternoon. It was still daylight. I was there in the immediate vicinity of Colonel Pavkovic, and in the course of the surrender, there was also Mr. Sljivancanin there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember how long it took for them to surrender?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: The process of surrender lasted until dusk. Now, I can't be more specific as to the exact time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Were you there throughout the surrender until the surrender was completed or not?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: I can't say that I was, because just before nightfall, I received the task to go to the location where the prisoners were put, and to tell the commander of the security detail that the prisoners should be treated in accordance with the rules, that nobody should be harmed in any way, and that everybody should take great care about their conduct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Who gave you this task?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: It was Mr. Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know where the people from the Mitnica Battalion had been taken to?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you start carrying out this task and what happened next?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Yes. I went there. It was dark by this time. When I arrived outside the building, which was a hangar, I asked right outside who their security commander was. The person I asked said it was he. I asked him to bring the commander of the Mitnica battalion, Filip Karaula. After this, I introduced myself, outside the hangar. I told him my name and my rank. I told this to the commander of the Mitnica Battalion, Filip Karaula and to the hangar security commander. I told them they should bear in mind that the ZNG soldiers should abstain from provoking the security inside the hangar in any way, on the one hand, and that the security men themselves should strictly abstain from any taunts or allowing themselves to be taunted by the captured members of the Mitnica Battalion in any way on the other. I then told the commander that if he believed it to be necessary, if he thought it was important, he should string a length of rope across the inside of the hangar, dividing the room inside the hangar in two. I told him to keep the Mitnica Battalion in one half and the security in the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karanfilov, you mentioned Filip Karaula. You were there for the surrender. During that time, did you speak to this man named Karaula?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Yes. That's where I'd met him. After the surrender itself, he was brought to the place where Mr. Pavkovic was, as well as Mr. Sljivancanin. The person who brought him there said that this was the commander of the Mitnica Battalion. He asked to be allowed to keep his knife, to keep this small knife, which his father had given to him. After this, Mr. Sljivancanin said it was okay for him to keep the knife and a hand-held radio set, so that he could carry on his work as commander overseeing the surrender of his own unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karanfilov, the day you went to Ovcara to the surrender, you spoke to this man who introduced himself as someone who was in charge of the security. Was this a military officer?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Yes. It was a military officer, quite short.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What about his rank? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: I think he was a captain.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did that officer tell you anything about any problems concerning the persons he was securing, at least at the time you were there?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: On the day when the Mitnica Battalion surrendered, how long did you stay in the area where they were put up? What would you think?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Ten or 15 minutes at the very most.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What happens next, do you remember? What did you do next?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: After that, I drove back to Negoslavci, to the office there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you report to anyone about this, specifically, did you inform Sljivancanin about the task you'd been given?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: I think I informed him that night, at some point, and he told me that the next morning I should be there for the taking away of the Mitnica Battalion from the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What about the next day? I'm not talking about dates. I'm talking about what happened. The surrender occurred on the 18th, which means that your task was on the 19th. The next day, did you follow that task, the task you'd been given by Mr. Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: The next day, I went to the hangar where I saw buses lined up, buses that had arrived earlier on. Food was being distributed, and people were boarding those buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell what time of day it was when you got there, when you got to this place where the members of the so-called Mitnica Battalion were being loaded on to buses?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: I think it was about 9.00 or 10.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see the officer you'd spoken to the previous evening at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Yes. I saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see anyone else you could identify, not by name perhaps but by affiliation to any of the units there, somebody who was there?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: I'm not sure about Besirevic but I know that the ICRC man was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You say you arrived there when food was being distributed and persons were being loaded on to buses. How long did the whole thing take? What do you think?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: I can't remember whether I actually stayed there until the buses left. Roughly speaking, I stayed there for about an hour or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: If I may just ask you a question, Mr. Karanfilov, when the Mitnica Battalion were being surrendered or were surrendering, was anybody compiling any lists of the people surrendering, for as long as you were there?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: On the 18th, when you got there, did you ask to see a list of the Mitnica Battalion when you got there on the 18th?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: You're talking about the day of the surrender?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What about the next day, when people were boarding those buses? Did you ask to see any sort of list at all or did you hear any references being made to lists?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: I know that as people were boarding the buses, somebody asked to draw up a list, one for each of the buses, or perhaps a general list. Was it the ICRC man or someone else, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: So was there a list?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: I asked the security commander if a list had been compiled. He said he did have one, a handwritten one. I asked him to have it typed up, if possible, and forwarded to either the ICRC or to the commander escorting the buses. I can't quite remember which.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if he did this or not?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: I don't. I don't know if he did this or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karanfilov, did you have any role to play at all in driving those persons to Sremska Mitrovica on those buses?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: No, no role at all. I didn't even know they were headed to Sremska Mitrovica. I'd heard about Sremska Mitrovica as I was lingering about the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: This man you said appeared to be in charge of security, was he a member of the Guards Brigade or a different unit? Do you know which unit?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: I knew for sure he wasn't from the Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to this one officer who you say was a captain, were there any other officers there on the day the Mitnica Battalion surrendered or the next day when they were taken to Sremska Mitrovica? Is this something you remember?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: On the day of their surrender, with the exception of him and the representative of the Mitnica Battalion, there was no one else. The next day, around the buses, there were people, officers, people wearing uniforms. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You say you weren't sure you were there for the actual departure of the buses. Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: I went to Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: When you left the hangar with those people who had been put up, did you notice a crowd or any sort of commotion or vehicles anywhere near the hangar, anything that would suggest that the environment was not a perfectly peaceful one conditionally speaking?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: No. Not a crowd of people really but there were a number of vehicles parked there to one side.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can you specify the distance between the hangar and the vehicles?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Several hundred metres, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you speak to anyone from the ICRC again or anyone else during the surrender or the next day, when the people were loaded on to those buses?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: I'm truly sorry, I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any other contact with those people whom you had seen on the 19th, during the boarding of the buses?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: On those days, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What about the list of the Mitnica Battalion that you were shown by the captain?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: It was written by hand in a notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: On the evening of the 18th, when the Mitnica Battalion surrendered, you suggest you talked to that officer and to the commander of the surrendering units. If I understand you correctly, you introduced yourself by giving them your first and last names and your rank. Why did you do that?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: The reason I introduced myself was because I was a JNA officer, an honourable officer. I thought this was an honourable thing to do vis-a-vis a prisoner of war or anyone else for that matter. When you talk to someone, you introduce yourself. You tell them your name, you tell them your rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you, at the time, perhaps, talk to that captain? Did you talk in order to advise him where he could find you, just in case he needed you?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: No, but there was no need for anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karanfilov, the 19th, that's the day, I'm not using any more dates for your sake. The buses left, people were boarding the buses, and you went back to Negoslavci. What time of day could this possibly have been?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: 12.00 noon, 1.00 p.m., possibly 2.00, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What about your drive back to Negoslavci? Do you remember your drive back to Negoslavci because of something in particular?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Yes. On my way back, in Negoslavci, I met Lieutenant-Colonel Djukic, who was our second in command in terms of counter-intelligence work. My second in command and Sljivancanin's first in command. And that's why I remembered this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain what the circumstances were of this meeting? You were someone in charge of the roadblocks, so did you ask him what he was doing there?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, Lieutenant-Colonel Djukic was standing next to an armoured fighting vehicle. We spoke very briefly, just a couple of minutes, and he told me on that occasion that he had -- he was escorting Mr. Cyrus Vance.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see Mr. Vance in Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how long Mr. Djukic and the entourage stayed there?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: We parted after a couple of minutes, but that would be approximately -- I think they left quite soon after this conversation, but I can't be more precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: On the 19th, did you have any other activities apart from the regular daily activities?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: I do recall that sometime -- it was in fact quite late, after nightfall, I was given a task by Mr. Sljivancanin to prepare a room for Mrs. Vesna Bosanac, and to receive Marin Vidic when he was brought in. So this was the task that I was given.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: And were Marin Vidic and Vesna Bosanac in fact brought in?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: I found a room in Negoslavci, through a nurse who worked at the hospital, and upon my return, I found Marin in the office where we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who had brought Marin Vidic and Vesna Bosanac to Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you inquire?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What was the building where you found Marin Vidic? Was that the building where the headquarters of the security organ were located or in another building?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: That was the building which housed not only the headquarters of the security organ but the headquarters of several other organs of the Guards Brigade, and this is where they were -- where he had been brought to, to the place where we were, to our office.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Was the Guards Brigade command housed in the same building?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Where was it, then?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: The command was located in another building, some 500 metres or maybe a kilometre away from the place where we were, our house.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: When you saw Marin Vidic, was anyone else present there from the security organ in the room?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: At first, there was Zoran Momcilovic, Mladen Karan and myself in the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What was the reason for Marin Vidic to be brought to your place?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: The reason was because an interview was to be conducted with him, with Marin Vidic, Bili, in order to gather some more information that would be important for the counter-intelligence work, for the counter-intelligence service, or for the Guards Brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know who Marin Vidic, Bili, was at all?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, he was the first man in Vukovar, politically speaking, the number 1 political figure in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: And did you actually conduct this interview? Did you talk to him? How did this proceed?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: The interview did not take place right away, because Marin himself said that he would like to eat something, he was hungry. He was given food, drinks, and as a result, the atmosphere in the office became quite relaxed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember any conversation with him, how -- what was his attitude towards you, towards the army in general?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: I think that he at one point started criticising the Croatian leadership, the ZNG, and at one point he became very negative towards the Croatian leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall if anyone else was present there? You mentioned warrant officer Momcilovic, Major Karan, yourself. Was anyone else present there during this conversation with Mr. Vidic?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin was there, and he actually conducted the interview for a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know Mr. Tumanov?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know Mr. Aleksandar Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: On that evening, when you had this interview with Marin Vidic, did you see Mr. Tumanov or Mr. Vasiljevic in this building?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I can remember, Colonel Tumanov walked in a little bit before General Vasiljevic did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Is there anything that makes you remember Colonel Tumanov's appearance there?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that because, after his arrival, Colonel Tumanov shook hands with all of us present there, and when he extended his hand to Marin Vidic, Bili, and when he was told this was Bili, he pulled his hand back suddenly, said he didn't want to greet a murderer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see if General Vasiljevic entered this room or not?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Yes. He went in after Tumanov.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: And how long did they stay there, I mean Mr. Vasiljevic and Mr. Tumanov?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: I can't recall, but I know that there was a conversation between General Vasiljevic and Major Sljivancanin. This was a fairly heated conversation. But I don't know how long they actually stayed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know the contents of the heated debate or did you not pay any attention?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: No, I don't know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karanfilov, how did this interview with Mr. Vidic end? You said you had given him some food, something to drink. Was there anything of interest there?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: After a while, after Mr. Sljivancanin had been talking to -- with him for a certain period of time, Marin Vidic, Bili, was taken to the office next door, where members of the criminal investigations unit continued or, rather, started their interview with him and the other crime investigation activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Marin Vidic have any items in his possession that were rather unusual?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Yes. He had his guitar with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: And was this guitar in fact put to some use while we are on the topic of the guitar?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Yes. As we ate and drank, he played the guitar and he sang and I have to say he was quite good.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karanfilov, you said that Mr. Marin Vidic was handed over to the crime investigation team. What was the reason for that?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Well, these are the people who actually interview persons in order to establish facts relating to crimes, to the commission of crimes. They try to find evidence of crimes, secure the evidence and so on. So the interview, in fact, continued, and the purpose was to establish the sites where crimes were committed and where people had been killed in Vukovar and to establish his role in those incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any other contacts with Vidic that night?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: The interviews took place in the same building or in another building? I mean, the interview conducted by the crime investigation unit.

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: It was in the same building.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karanfilov, that evening, when Mr. Vidic was brought in, do you remember if you were given any tasks for the next day and, if yes, what tasks did you receive? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Yes. The task that was received from Mr. Sljivancanin, and as far as I can remember, we were told that on the orders of General Vasiljevic, we were to go to the shelter or, rather, Jastreb's command post the next morning, to -- and to transfer all documents of any interest urgently to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who Jastreb is? Let us clarify that.

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Jastreb was the commander of the National Guard Corps in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Who, in the security organ, received this task from Mr. Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did any other officers in the security organ receive any other tasks from him? If you know.

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Well, as regards this task, the removal of the documents, I was given this task, and warrant officer Momcilovic was also given this task together with me. As far as I can remember, Karan was told that he should accompany him the next day. I don't remember about anything else but that would be more or less it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear where Karan was supposed to accompany Mr. Sljivancanin the next day?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, they were talking about the evacuation of the hospital, and Karan was supposed to accompany him to prepare all the security aspects of the evacuation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember if you had any information as to who was actually in the Vukovar Hospital, apart from the sick people, of course?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: We had been receiving information or reports that many ZNG members had changed their clothes and pretending that they were actually patients but that they still carried arms and that they were still in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember if you received any such information while Marin Bilic [as interpreted] was in Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: I think, yes, I remember that there were reports that the shelter could be booby-trapped, so we did receive reports to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You said to prepare for appropriate security. What does it mean?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: In light of the data at our disposal, to select the -- to pick out the persons who were in the hospital but who were not wounded or sick. In other words, people who were in fact members of combat units. And to make sure that the weapons held there would not be actually used.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: And was this in fact one of the tasks of the security organ, to make sure that those security conditions were in place?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: After receiving those tasks, did you have any other tasks to carry out that night or did you just receive your tasks for the next day?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: No. We didn't have any other tasks for that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would now like to move on to another topic and perhaps this would be a proper time for us to take our first break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bulatovic. We'll resume at 10 past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karanfilov, let us please continue our conversation. Let's pick up where we left off. On the evening of the 19th, you were told to go to Jastreb's shelter to get whatever documents you found there as well as a number of other things. Did you carry out that particular task and can you please describe the progress of that task? How exactly did you carry it out? Please tell us -- give us a steady account.

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Yes. The following morning, Zoran Momcilovic and I were supposed to go to that shelter but we didn't know where it was, so we tried to get in touch with the forensic technicians who had been sent there to inspect the premises the night before. We were told that the technicians had gone on to the hospital with Marin Vidic, Bili. So the two of us went. However, at the hospital gate, we were met by one of the officers. We asked him about the forensic technicians and he told us that they had left for the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karanfilov, can you specify the time? Was this in the morning or in the afternoon that you were off to this assignment?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: That was in the morning, at about 10.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: After that, we returned to the barracks and we found the forensic technicians there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Please pause there. Did you see buses within the barracks?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Yes. There were buses inside. The buses were full of people, and around those buses there was a group of people abusing those on the buses verbally.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember how many buses there were?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: A total of three or four. I can't say exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You say there was a group of people around the buses. How large was that group?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Between 40 and 50 people, predominantly men.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Were those men wearing uniform or civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: It was a mixed group. There were different kinds of uniforms and civilians there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Was anyone from that group armed?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Yes, people were armed in that group.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please describe the scene and tell us what was going on?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: There was a cordon of military police set up around those buses. So there was no contact between the buses and the group of between 40 and 50 people that I described. The only thing that was going on was a lot of verbal abuse, taunts, curses, that's about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see any other vehicles there, apart from the buses, within the barracks? Anywhere near the buses?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: You mean military vehicles or civilian?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Just around the buses.

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: No, none.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I assume there should be a number of military vehicles in any barracks, so I'm just talking about the area where the buses were. Did you see any officers around the buses? If so, did you speak to any of them?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: I saw Lieutenant-Colonel Lukic. If I'm not mistaken, he was the barracks commander. We talked for a couple of minutes about what was going on. You see, he said, some minor problems, insults, jeers, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karanfilov, when you saw the buses, when you saw the people on the buses, did you know where those people were from or did you perhaps assume?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: I don't know if I was right or not, but after that meeting with Mr. Sljivancanin, my inference was that these were the people from the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What about Lieutenant-Colonel Lukic, the barracks commander, the person you spoke to? Did he perhaps say that he could use some sort of assistance or that he sought assistance from you? Did he complain that the situation was far more serious than the way it appeared to you at the time?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: No. He didn't. Nor did I have the impression that he was in need of something. He certainly didn't tell me. Quite the opposite, in fact. The impression was he was keeping everything under control and there were no exceptional problems that would require any measures being taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You were now in the barracks to look for the forensic technicians so you could be off to that shelter, right? How long did you stay there for?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Hardly more than 15 or 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: All right. What happens next?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: I first spoke to Lukic and then the forensic technicians drove by. Rather, there was a driver in front of the car, and behind. I asked them whether they had been successful in locating the shelter, and they said yes. We followed them so that they could show us where the shelter was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you eventually reach the shelter and what did you do next?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: In addition to the forensic men, there was someone else in the vehicle, I don't remember who. They took us as far as the shelter, stopped outside the shelter, dropped us there and left. They didn't actually enter together with us. Momcilovic and I went as far as the door. There was a jacket of sorts hanging there, no electricity. When we entered the shelter, there was a huge plane bomb or a missile on the table. We weren't really sure and we had been told that the place might be booby-trapped in its entirety so we -- [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphones for the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: So we didn't use any torches or anything, just in case the place was booby-trapped.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karanfilov, these electric torches that you refer to, what do these have to do with any booby-traps that were inside the shelter?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Those can be electricity-activated, so several minutes after we had left, an engineer arrived and went straight into the shelter. I don't know exactly how much time had elapsed but he told us that we could just go on and do our work. Momcilovic and I went inside and did what we had to do. We got the things, we got the documents, the logs, the books, some notebooks, some directories, anything that we found to be of interest. I think we collected two or three radio sets, hand-held ones. I know we got a video tape too, possibly two, a floppy disk. That was what we found there that we could use that had not been burned down.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Were all of these things still whole and intact or had some of it burned down previously?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: On the whole, one could notice that there had been a fire inside this shelter, one that was started deliberately. Most of the equipment and items in there had either burned down altogether or had at least caught fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: So among the documents that you eventually picked up, were there any documents that had been damaged by this fire to any extent?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: There was this diary or a log, the cover of which was singed but the actual diary, the pages inside, were still preserved.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What about those radio sets? Were there any other radio sets inside?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Yes. There were quite a number of them, military ones of foreign make.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Was there a particular reason for you to take these away, the hand-held radio sets, I mean?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: We weren't looking for JNA radio stations. We were on the other hand looking for hand-held ones, the sort used more by the Ministry of the Interior, so that we could get at their frequencies. We needed those radio stations to establish the channels and the crystals used by those radio sets.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You mean the ZNG units, right, those used by the ZNG units?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karanfilov, you say you were in the hospital between 10.00 and 11.00, you stayed for 10 or 15 minutes, no more. You went back to the shelter. How long did it take you to do all of that, get the documents, pack the things? How long did it take you?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Everything that could be of use to us was put in two or three black bin bags, and now, as for how long it took to do all that, I don't know. I know that we departed from the shelter to Belgrade while it was still daylight, so 3.00, half past 3.00, 4.00 tops.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you encounter anyone there at the shelter, any officers or anyone else?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: We met Mr. Sljivancanin near the shelter. On that occasion, we told him that we had taken the items that in our estimate should have been taken, and he told us that we should transport it to Belgrade urgently, by air.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karanfilov, after you removed those hand sets and documents from the shelter, was any equipment still in the shelter, any materiel? Do you remember anything at all?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Quite a lot of equipment remained in the shelter, weapons, ammunition, equipment, radio equipment that had been damaged by fire, quite a lot of stuff remained there, but as I have already noted, this was of no interest for us in the counter-intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: So you estimate that you completed your task sometime around half past 3.00, around 4.00, while it was still daylight and then you met Sljivancanin and did you report to him and told him that you had gathered all that?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Yes. We told him that we had removed the items that in our opinion should be taken away and he told us that we should go to Belgrade urgently and hand these over to the security administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: And did you go to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Immediately after that?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: I think that we stayed in Negoslavci for a short while. If I remember correctly, warrant officer Momcilovic was supposed to take something with him or leave something there, but after about ten minutes, we left.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: And when did you get to Belgrade or, rather, how long would it take to you get from Vukovar to Belgrade in those circumstances?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: We arrived there at night. It may have been up to two and a half to three hours of driving. That's how long it took you to drive to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: At what time could it have been, in your estimate?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Around 7.00 p.m., 1900 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: And what did you do with the documents and radio sets that you had taken from the shelter?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: The documents were handed over, as soon as we got to Belgrade, to the duty operations officer in the security administration. So everything that we had taken with us, we handed over to the operations team, and we stayed there for maybe an hour. We had coffee with the people and there were some informal conversation, and then the two of us, or, rather, Momcilovic took me home and then he drove on to his own home.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you go back to Vukovar at all after this?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Let me be more specific. Do you know when your brigade returned from Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: We did not go back because the next day we were told there was no need for us because the brigade would be coming back any way in a couple of days. So there was no need for us to go back there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karanfilov, do you remember -- you said that you arrived there that night, but do you remember the next day, whether you were actually in the brigade?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: The next day, sometime in the afternoon, after taking some rest, we left and we met warrant officer Grocic there, and he told us that the brigade commander was there in Belgrade, so that we were in the brigade that afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any information as to why the brigade commander was there on that day?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, the brigade commander had had a meeting with the federal secretary, as far as I can recall. That's what we were told.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: And who was the federal secretary?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: That was General Veljko Kadijevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how many days after your arrival from Vukovar did the brigade arrive there?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Four to five days. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: In the two, three or -- to five days, did you go from Belgrade to Vukovar? I'm talking only about those three, four or five days?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karanfilov, there is a time line of the events that you talked about but now let me address some other issues. How many times were you in the location that we know was Ovcara, which was the location where the members of the so-called Mitnica Battalion were placed during your stay in Vukovar? So how many times were you there?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Two times. The first time was in the evening when we were given the suggestion, and the next morning, when those prisoners were put on the buses and taken out of the hangars and driven away in those buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karanfilov, you are an officer in the security organ. Did you have any subordinates? Did you have anyone that you were a superior officer to?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: No, no. The security organ is structured in the following way. You have the chief, two deputies, and the officer who is at the same level, and that's regardless of the ranks.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: So who was your superior?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: My superior was Mr. Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: And who gave you tasks in the service?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: It was Mr. Sljivancanin or, in fact, at that time, it was Mr. Karan, but subject to the approval of Mr. Sljivancanin, if the task pertained to the counter-intelligence work.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you file any reports regarding your tasks and the completion of those tasks and who did you actually report to?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: I submitted my counter-intelligence reports orally to Mr. Karan, who was then -- whose task it was to write the information I gave him down.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who those reports were submitted to? So you reported to Mr. Karan and then who did Mr. Karan submit those reports to?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: According to our chain of command, the reports could only be submitted to the security chief of the cabinet of the federal secretary.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karanfilov, while you were in Vukovar, did you ever see or hear of the security organ in the Guards Brigade receiving the reports from the security organs of any other unit?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: No, with the exception of the security administration. No, as far as I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You, as an officer in the security organ, do you have the right to issue orders to members of units?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did anyone ever -- ever ask you -- I mean from the Guards Brigade, officers from the Guards Brigade, to relay an order to anyone, an order that would pertain to some other unit?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karanfilov, does the name Vezmarovic mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Yes. That was the name that was put to me in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: When did you first hear this name, Vezmarovic?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: I think it was in 2001, when I was making a statement to the military investigating judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Let us go back to the first day, your first contact with the captain securing the Mitnica Battalion troops at the location that you described to us. You told us what Mr. Sljivancanin had told you. How would you describe the -- the words that you relayed to this commander? What was that?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: That would be a preventive activity by the security organ. Most of the activities of our service are based on preventive action. Preventive action and guidance. Exclusively, solely preventive action.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Would this be an order?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: No, it was not an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karanfilov, did you ever hear Mr. Sljivancanin issue an order to anyone apart from his security organs or of him doing that?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karanfilov, let me ask you: How many statements have you made regarding these events in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Eight statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember who you gave those statements to, those eight statements?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: The security administration of the Yugoslav People's Army, the investigating judge from a military court, the investigators from the OTP, the Novi Sad court investigating judge, the administration for the struggle against organised crime, twice in court in Belgrade, in the Ovcara case, and then once again I made the statement to the OTP investigator.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
