utterances.text: Mr. Karanfilov, on those occasions when you made those eight statements, has anyone, any of the investigators, or any of the persons who questioned you as a witness, shown you any document or anything pertaining to the events from that period?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: No. I was not -- I have not been shown any documents, any reports, and I have never been shown any of the statements that I had made on previous occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: When was the first time that you saw any military documents or any materials pertaining to this period?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: The day before yesterday. That was the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: When? How?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: I saw those documents as I was preparing for my testimony in -- at your place.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have no further questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bulatovic. Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. Good afternoon, Mr. Karanfilov. I will ask you the same thing that my learned colleague, Mr. Bulatovic, did, to make a pause between answering after I finish my question so that everything is interpreted and everything is in the transcript. Mr. Karanfilov, you told my learned colleague that you drove to Belgrade. Can you please tell us what vehicle did you use while you were in Vukovar and what vehicle did you use to get back to Belgrade, as you just described to us?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: I went to Belgrade in a Puh with police marks, and with the lights, the police lights.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But let me just clarify for everyone in the courtroom. Puh, that would be an all terrain vehicle, not a sedan; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell me -- I see here in your evidence here and in the statements that you've given over all those years, that you have trouble remembering the actual dates, but that you do remember the events. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: I remember the events but not the dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And in the period between 1998, when you said you gave your first statement, you tried to remember as many things as possible relating to the questions that you were asked about these events and in the proceedings?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean by making special effort. You do your daily job, you get summoned to make a statement, you do it, and then you go back to your job. So I don't know what you mean when you say that I was trying to remember as many things as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You told my colleague that you saw some documents for the first time when you came here. Can you please tell us what were those documents that you saw in order to refresh your memory about those events, from the surrender of the Mitnica Battalion onwards?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I saw a lot of video footage, and the diaries kept by various commands, some notes, some orders, and that would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When you looked through all those notes, did you find any references to your own activities, about Marin Vidic, Bili, Jastreb's headquarters or carrying those documents back to Belgrade? Did you find any references to that?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Not sure I understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I'll be glad to repeat it for your benefit. You say you watched certain video footage, you looked at diaries, at orders, as well as other documents. Did you come across anything that would jog your memory about any steps that you took at the time, anything you did about Mitnica, about Marin Vidic, Bili, or about going to Jastreb's headquarters or perhaps about taking those documents to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: I saw a reference about Cyrus Vance. That's one thing that I saw in the notes. And after so many years, this tells me that the chief of security of the cabinet of the federal secretary was there which shed a lot of new light on the incident, and this had already been forgotten.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You've provided a great many statements. It's very difficult to keep track of everything. Therefore, let me ask the usher to hand copies of your statements to you and to distribute these self-same copies to the Trial Chamber and my learned friends from the OTP so that I could start using these in my examination-in-chief, please. I hope we all have those now. Thank you. Mr. Karanfilov, if you look at page 1 of the report, your statements, there is an overview of the actual content. As soon as necessary, we shall be asking you to look at certain tabs. Sir, do you agree with me that you gave your first statement back in 1998, to the security organ? And that between that first statement and the next statement you gave, there had elapsed three years, the statement to the investigating magistrate of the Belgrade court? Would I be right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: I'm not sure by being that specific about this. Be that as it may, my first statement was indeed to the security administration back in 1998, if I'm not mistaken. And the next one occurred in 2002 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Correction for the transcript. The transcript says "2002" and the witness said "2001." I didn't mean to imply anything by being specific about the time lag between the two statements. I'm just trying to suggest that you did not provide any statements over that period. After that, you gave a statement in July 2003 to the administration for the struggle against organised crime, which is part of the Serbian Ministry of the Interior; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: This statement actually preceded the one you provided in November 2003 to the investigating magistrate --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I don't mean to interrupt. I see my learned friend refers to July 2003. I don't know if that's intentionally -- or not intentional, but an error. I notice his statement says March 2003 and certainly March 2003 is the date that we have in our bundle.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure which document my learned friend has in mind when he describes it as being dated March 2003. As for the statement to the Ministry of the Interior, the date is the 18th of July 2003. The statement to the investigating magistrate of the Novi Sad district court is dated the 5th of November, 2003. If that's of any assistance to my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, there are some audio-recorded interviews in March 2003. Are you passing those over?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe these are the audiotapes of his statement to OTP investigators. I wasn't going to invoke those right now, but I think that is dated March 2003, and not the statement provided to the military court or indeed the special court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, the problem was you introduced all of this having got a statement in 2001. You then said after that you gave a statement in July 2003. I don't see any reference anywhere to July 2003 in the index. There are the four audiotapes to the OTP in March 2003, and then we have the Belgrade military court on the 5th of November 2003. Is there some other statement that you haven't included in this bundle?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour. This statement is not included in the bundle because we do not have a translation. It's just about the exact sequence. That statement preceded the statement to the investigating magistrate of the Novi Sad district court on the 5th of November 2003.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karanfilov, can you please now go to tab 3, which is the statement that you provided to the investigating magistrate of the Novi Sad district court on the 5th of November, 2003. The ID number is 30465403. The ID number is 03465403. Tab 3. Have you got that, Mr. Karanfilov? You gave the statement that is recorded here. Is this your signature, sir?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I would like to talk about something that is at page 3 of the B/C/S. It's the first paragraph. I'll read it out and can you please follow just to make sure that that is indeed what the statement says. "Once I had conveyed these orders, I went back to the command. On the following day -- on the morning of the following day, I received a task of going to the Vukovar barracks and bringing back Marin Vidic, Bili, and Vesna Bosanac. When I reached the barracks, I saw several buses being secured by the army. There were people on those buses but I didn't know who they were. I'm not certain, but I think that I saw quite many civilians there and Territorial Defence members within the barracks compound who were voicing their displeasure. They abused and insulted those on the buses. "I stayed there for about 15 minutes and I did not see the situation as particularly dramatic. I think we relate this to Lukic who was the barracks commander, and I also seem to remember that we informed Sljivancanin upon our return to Negoslavci with Marin Vidic and Vesna Bosanac. On that day, we interviewed Marin Vidic. I know that several hours later, General Vasiljevic too arrived. I can't remember exactly when the questioning was completed, but it was at some point that evening. And I don't believe that I went anywhere else that late afternoon or that evening." Sir, is this what you said to the investigating magistrate?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: That's what it says, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you remember saying anything along these lines on the 1st of October 2002, to the investigating magistrate of the Belgrade military court?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Please, it is quite obvious that these incidents are mentioned in all the statements, and I mention all the individual incidents in all of my statements. I hadn't set eyes on a single document over all these years, so it is only logical, if you ask me, that events should be mis-timed, that two incidents should be erroneously referred to as happening on the same day, whereas that was in fact not the case. The simple truth of the matter is I am discussing the same events all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: The same events in the same way. Are you suggesting these things happened when you left to get Marin Vidic, Bili, and Vesna Bosanac and collect them from the barracks, right?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: The buses were inside the barracks. That appears to suggest that the interview with Marin Vidic, Bili, had occurred on the previous day. That's why I'm telling you it's been 15 years; it had been 12 at the time I gave that first statement. All this about the various meetings and the various time lines, I referred to all of that in all of my statements. I remember what happened. I remember the actual incidents, but not necessarily their dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I do agree with that. But will you agree with me, when I say, that in all these statements you gave, when talking about Marin Vidic, Bili, being taken from Vukovar to Negoslavci, you say that you saw buses inside the barracks compound, four or five buses and the group of people there? Do you agree that you said that?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: That's what it says. It is obvious that I was looking for the forensic technicians that Marin Vidic, Bili, had been with on that day, and the shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I agree. Yet I have to ask you this: In your testimony before the special court in Belgrade, on the 23rd of November, 2004, did you again say that you had seen the buses inside the barracks compound when you arrived to get Marin Vidic, Bili? Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Yes. That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you then agree with me that you informed of this particular situation within the barracks compound Major Lukic who was then the barracks commander, as well as Major Sljivancanin, once you were back in Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: You mean about the buses, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I mean.

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: I spoke to Mr. Lukic about that. I told him about that. It was a brief exchange. As for Mr. Sljivancanin, I believe I informed him when we met just before I was off to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: A daytime meeting, right?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You tell us about who spoke to Marin Vidic, Bili. Was someone interviewing Vesna Bosanac in Negoslavci at the same time after you had brought them there?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: I think it was Mr. Sljivancanin interviewing her.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps remember the specific room in which he interviewed Vesna Bosanac?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: I think it was one of the rooms at the command. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you remember when and if Mr. Sljivancanin returned to that house where you were too, and after that, was he involved in the interview with Marin Vidic, Bili?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: As I said, he showed up. Marin was already in our office. And sometime later, Major Sljivancanin too turned up. I'm not sure how long that took.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you go through the counter-intelligence procedure with Marin Vidic in light of the fact that he was a member of the Vukovar Defence Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Several hours were spent with Marin Vidic, Bili, for the purpose of adaptation. I know that Mladen Karan interviewed him as an expert and then Major Sljivancanin did too, but not in order to gain any counter-intelligence information, as you seem to be suggesting in your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And did you know what they were talking about?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, the topic, the main topic, was his political views and the causes for the conflict, his own personal views and attitude. Marin Vidic, Bili, was not a person -- he did not hold the kind of a post that would enable him to have any information important for the counter-intelligence work, because he was a politician.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me whether you were in the Vukovar Hospital, and if yes, when, and how long did you spend there?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: I was at the hospital gate. That was on the day when we tried to get in touch with the forensic technicians and Bili.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the time of the day?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: It was in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that if a witness were to give evidence that it was at 6.00 a.m., then it wouldn't be true?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: I don't know what a witness might or might not say. I was there at around 9, 10, 10, I don't know, that was the approximate time period.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us go back to the barracks and the events that you witnessed there, and that you reported about, both to Lukic and to Sljivancanin. In your opinion, were those events alarming in nature, in security terms?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: No. I don't know what would be your definition of "alarming in security terms."

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In your opinion, in fact, did you inform these people about the events because the situation was alarming, in terms of the security of the people within the barracks?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: I don't know where you get the information about the alarming situation from. As far as I was able to see, the buses were secure. A group of maybe 40 to 50 people were not right next to the buses. They were away from the buses, and they did not go beyond verbal abuse. Furthermore, as I already stated, I spoke to Mr. Lukic. Mr. Lukic had already seen that. He already had this information at his disposal. I agree that it was an unpleasant picture, an unusual one, but it was not alarming.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This is what you have stated before. I merely wanted to ask you about your opinion at the time when you were making this report. Now I would like you to tell us something about the notebook that you mentioned here, the notebook that you saw in the possession of this officer that was in charge of the security of the Mitnica group. Did you see what kind of notes he made there, or did you just see him carry this notebook, hold it in his hands?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: You're talking about the day when these people were boarded -- boarded the buses?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm talking about the day when the Mitnica group boarded the buses and left for Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: No. I did not hold the notebook in my hands. I was just told by him about the notes that he took and wrote down in this notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Does the name Lieutenant-Colonel Milorad Vojinovic mean anything to you and did it mean anything to you at that time?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: No, not at the time, not now either. I am not familiar with that name at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you hear this name in relation to the trial here in The Hague or the trials in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Yes. That's why I say I did not know of that day -- name at the time, and now, again, although I did hear it at the trials, now it doesn't mean anything to me either.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When this Mitnica group left the Ovcara hangar to go to Sremska Mitrovica, did you see Lieutenant-Colonel Vojinovic there? Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: I don't remember having seen the Lieutenant-Colonel at any time before that, after that, ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And Drago Vukosavljevic, does that name mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: The same answer. So the name was not known to me. It was mentioned in the proceedings, but it still doesn't mean anything to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the period that we are now talking about, the fall of 1991, if you remember, can you please tell us whether you went to Sid and on what business, if yes?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: No. I went to Sid only once, in 2002, with a high-ranking official, but that was the first time. I had never gone there before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell me: Do you remember, did Colonel Tumanov and General Vasiljevic, did they address Marin Vidic, and if yes, what did they talk about?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: I don't think so, with the exception of the incident, the brief incident, when Tumanov withdrew his hand. As far as I can remember, they didn't actually talk.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell me when you got to the barracks, where you saw the buses, who was with you at the time?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: You mean in the vehicle?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In the barracks.

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: It was Zoran Momcilovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell me whether there was any security or any check-point at the entrance to the barracks?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Yes, there was the reception booth and a swing gate.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us, if you remember, at the time when you were questioned about taking Marin Vidic to Negoslavci, whether that was at the same -- on the same day when the session of the government was held at Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as a matter of principle, Mr. Vasic said, "When you were questioned," and he didn't specify the occasion. The witness was -- gave eight statements and I think he should identify the occasion when he said that. I think that should be done in fairness towards this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, Your Honour. I will identify the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When you gave your statement to the military court investigating judge, that was the 1st of October, page 4. The investigating judge of the Novi Sad military court, Novi Sad district court, that would be page 3. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: As far as I was able to understand the thrust of your question, the question is whether I had stated that I had heard about any session being held.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: At the time when you were taking Marin Vidic and Vesna Bosanac to Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Let me repeat: In light of the time that has elapsed since the events, the events that I mention are described correctly in all my statements. The problem lies with the time line. This is what I can't recall. If you ask me whether on the day when I saw the buses, when I was there, somebody did mention something about a session.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Now I would like you to go to tab 3. That's the statement you gave to the investigating judge of the district court in Novi Sad. The number is 03 -- 03465403. Please look at the last sentence on this page. Let me read it out to you slowly.

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: What page?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Page 3.

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: "What I know about any alleged session of the civilian authorities is that at that time --"

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Tab 3?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Tab 3, that's the statement you gave to the investigating judge of the Novi Sad district court, dated 5 November 2003.

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Page 3?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Page 3. And at the end of the page, you say -- the second part of the last paragraph. "What I know about an alleged session of the civilian authorities is that at that time, when we took over the Mitnica battalion that had been captured, I heard that a session was being held just across the road from the barracks and that it was attended by Arkan. I didn't hear about any conclusions reached at that session or meeting. Let me be more specific. This session that I heard of took place on the day when the Mitnica Battalion surrendered, not on that day when the Mitnica Battalion surrendered, but the next day, when they boarded the buses, and on the day when I was tasked with bringing Marin Vidic and Vesna Bosanac." Do you agree with me that this is what you stated?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: That's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that a convenient time, Mr. Vasic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes. I would like us to take our break now. This is a convenient time. I don't have a lot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We resume at 10 minutes to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I'm nearing the end of my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karanfilov, back in November 1991, did you know that on the 19th of November, in the evening hours, from the security administration in the counter-intelligence group of the 1st Military District, two officer teams had arrived to conduct a triage and dispatch those suspected of having committed crimes to Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: No. I didn't know that, nor would I have been expected to know a thing like that given my rank and my post at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just another question. Do you know if any suspects detained during the actual combat were sent to Sid? Is this something that you might have been familiar with at the time?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: No, it isn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Just to be fair, no?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: No. No, it was above my head.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Now it's crystal clear. Thank you. Mr. Karanfilov, I have no further questions for you and I thank you for all your answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. This concludes my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasic. Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Karanfilov, why didn't you tell the court in your evidence in chief that you had informed Mr. Sljivancanin of what you saw at the barracks, the bad behaviour at the barracks? Why didn't you tell them?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: I don't think I was asked, was I?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But you gave an account of what you saw and the fact that you'd spoken to Sljivancanin; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: My apologies. Could you please repeat that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. You had told the Bench, as it's called, Their Honours, that you had seen the behaviour at the barracks. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And I think it's right to say that you'd also told them that you saw Sljivancanin on the 20th as well, afterwards; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Yes, I did say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm just asking why it is you didn't mention the fact, as indeed you have done now, that you told Sljivancanin about the trouble at the barracks. Didn't you think that was an important piece of evidence to tell the Bench?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: I didn't take that to be a major problem. I didn't believe that to be a source of major trouble at the barracks at the time but I do remember that. I did say on numerous occasions that I had informed Mr. Sljivancanin about that, and if I'm not entirely mistaken, I did answer a question by one of the counsel about that a while ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, you did. But I'm just asking you why it is, if you're here to assist the Court, as an honest and true man, why you didn't tell them that when you spoke to Sljivancanin I told him about the trouble at the barracks. And I'm merely asking, was that just an oversight or was it deliberate?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: It certainly wasn't deliberate. I think what I was doing was focusing on the question regarding me leaving the shelter. So believe me, there was no particular intention on my part.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You would agree, wouldn't you, that in any evacuation, that if there is behaviour seen in the presence of that evacuation, behaviour that would suggest concern, behaviour that might suggest hostility, that that is an element that should be communicated to someone in authority? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Again, what I have to say is this: The situation at the barracks was not alarming, just as counsel suggested a while ago, nor did I have the impression that this was in any way out of control. On the other hand, the barracks commander was present. The commander was there. I talked to him and I got the impression and realised that he was keeping everything under control.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But do you remember the briefing of the 19th of November with Mr. Sljivancanin? Do you remember there was normally a security organ briefing after the command briefing? I think that's right, as a general rule, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Not necessarily in the security organ. Any intelligence related observation on what was going on on the ground concerning organisations or individuals or anything that our intelligence work yielded, could have been reported to Karan, in Sljivancanin's absence, for example. Therefore, meetings were not held on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Was there a meeting held on the evening of the 19th of November, a meeting where Mr. Sljivancanin briefed other members of the security organ?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what members of the security organ were present at the briefing of the evening of the 19th?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: So we are talking about the meeting of the evening that Marin Vidic was there. This meeting, this brief meeting was attended by Karan, Momcilovic, and I.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What would you say if in actual fact there had been evidence given that there was a briefing on the evening of the 19th for all the members of the security organ, including Vukasinovic?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Not that I remember. It is possible that it's just me not being able to remember Vukasinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, you were aware, weren't you, that Vukasinovic was responsible, was he not, for putting people on the bus at the hospital? Weren't you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So you don't remember a briefing on the night of the 19th where actually Vukasinovic was the first person to be briefed and then had to leave and other tasks were given out? Are you saying you weren't present at that particular briefing?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: What I'm saying is I remember the three of us being there the day the meeting was held. Did Vukasinovic attend another meeting before that one is not something that I can say. Did he have an assignment likewise, I can't say and I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So as far as you're concerned, you do not remember attending a briefing on the 19th, a briefing given by Mr. Sljivancanin, to members of the security organ, including Vukasinovic? Is that what your evidence is?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: What I'm saying is I don't remember Vukasinovic being there. I was in and out of the meeting, perhaps, so it's certainly possible. But the only persons I remember as being there are the three that I've mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The tasks given on the 19th, what were those tasks, in very shortened form? Can you just tell us, please? I presume these tasks were the following day for the 20th. So what were the tasks?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: What I remember is as follows: Momcilovic's task and mine was to go get any documents that were related in intelligence terms and take it straight to Belgrade. I remember that Karan was to leave with Mr. Vukasinovic the following morning. I also remember mention being made of the hospital evacuation. It was also said that security measures should be taken for the evacuation and during the actual evacuation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we agree that there was a briefing in relation to the evacuation of the hospital? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Evacuation was one of the things discussed at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So if we just deal with that topic, the briefing on the 19th, one of the topics was the evacuation; is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what role did you play in the evacuation?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: None.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What role did Mr. Karan play in the evacuation?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Apart from the fact that he was to leave the next day with Mr. Sljivancanin, there was nothing else that I knew of.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But what were they to do? They may well leave, but what was their function, what was their task, the next day?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: I know nothing about the task except for what I specified. If I may, the security organ receives assignments from its superior, but only assignments within its actual remit and authority. This is very specifically defined in the work of security officers. No security organ can know anything about the assignments of any other security organ unless the chief decides otherwise, but not the direct superior but, rather, the second in command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But the situation is this: There was a briefing by the chief of the security organ on the 19th. We've had evidence in relation to that. You were present at that briefing. And might I be so bold as to suggest that one of the purposes of briefing is to let everybody know what their individual tasks are? And I'm asking you what were the tasks assigned to Karan, and, of course, Mr. Sljivancanin? What were the words? What were they to do?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Sljivancanin was the one handing out tasks, with the exception of the task to set up a security regime for the evacuation, but that's all I know about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I will almost -- I have almost finished this topic. I may come back to it. So you were present at the briefing. What I want to know is quite simply this: There was talk about the evacuation of the hospital; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Among other things, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm just talking about the evacuation of the hospital. What were the component parts for the evacuation of the hospital? Who was responsible for who? Who was coordinating with whom?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: I don't know, nor was anything said about that in my presence, except I remember that Karan was to go with Sljivancanin to the hospital the next morning to set up security for the evacuation. That's all I knew about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Are you aware or have you been told by Mr. Bulatovic, who I think has proofed you, about the possibility of the existence of lists being compiled by the security organ prior to the hospital evacuation?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: As far as you're aware, is it right to say that the security organ was attempting to find out the names of individuals whom they held responsible for what I will call "the situation in Vukovar," namely, the defenders, the people who were fighting against the JNA?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: We didn't see them as defenders. In practical terms, yes. Counter-intelligence can yield names, identities and persons who are potential perpetrators of crimes or criminal offences against any soldier, civilians or the JNA itself and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So when you say quite simply that you didn't see them as defenders, from your perception, and I don't criticise it in any way, from your perception, the people who were fighting against you were generically criminals, would that be right?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Please, sir. Back in 1991, there was the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia. There was the JNA. Everything that was outside the constitution of the SFRY was a form of rebellion, certainly a criminal offence. The JNA, under the constitution, was duty-bound to protect the constitutional order of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But I'm asking you, and thank you for that, with regard to the perception in 1991, the people that you were looking for, you considered to be potential perpetrators of crimes and committers of criminal offences. That is right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: A perpetrator of a criminal offence or a rebel in purely legal terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We have heard the word "terrorist" in this Court. Would you accept that they were often considered to be terrorists, analogous to terrorists?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: You could put it that way, as a blanket term, terrorist, an insurgent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. And isn't it right that lists were being compiled, names were being collected, of these people? Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, we have seen evidence coming in through the SSNO and the security administration, security organ, of various names. I will take them -- you to those names tomorrow if I have to, but weren't you aware, as a member of the security organ in your various briefings, that that's the sort of person that you were looking for?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: No. My only responsibility was in Negoslavci, with the village of Berak included.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But it's right to say you were a member, an officer, in the security organ and there were briefings almost every day? Is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Yes. I was an officer in the security organ. Meetings did not take place every day; it depended on the situation. Again, a security organ is informed of elements that are essential to the implementation of its task, but not necessarily everything. The chief is the person who knows the entire situation, who knows what the counter-intelligence assessment is or any information trickling down from the higher spheres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, you're aware that we've had evidence from Mr. Sljivancanin and also others from the security organ. Let us take a ten-day period. It's difficult to approximate, I know. If one was talking about a ten-day period in October-November, how often would you have briefings from the security organ or the commander of the security organ?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: First and foremost, I don't know what Mr. Sljivancanin said. Secondly, I can't be specific because this was a wartime situation. It was changing on an hourly basis. Meetings were held whenever the situation allowed. Any intelligence reports on the security situation that were important to the brigade command were dispatched urgently, no meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, may I finish this topic on the following question? Would it be right to say or would you agree with me that there were regular meetings with the security organ officers in Vukovar in October and November?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: If regular means daily, then the answer is no. It very much depended on the situation at hand. You could have had two meetings in two days and you could have had a single meeting no more over a ten-day period.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May I move to the 18th of November? Because you have difficulty with dates, that's the Mitnica evacuation, all right?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: We are talking about the surrender of the Mitnica Battalion, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, the Mitnica unit. Why do you call it a battalion?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: We are talking about the Mitnica Battalion and you're asking me why I'm calling it a battalion?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Because that's how it was introduced to us, and it was the battalion type of unit, and Filip Karaula, establishment-wise, was a battalion commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So would it be right to say that attributing to them the term "battalion" ensured that they were what I will call soldiers who have laid down their arms and should be dealt with appropriately under the Geneva Convention?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: All those from the Mitnica Battalion who surrendered were to be and indeed were treated in keeping with all the regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And isn't it right that there was a distinction drawn between what I will call the Mitnica or you call the Mitnica Battalion and a group of individuals, fighters, who had retreated to the hospital and had to be identified? Would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: The unit that surrendered, in terms of establishment, belonged to the ZNG. And the treatment that they received was in compliance with all the rules and regulations. All those who fled laid down their arms, discarded their weapons and disguised themselves, and yet had committed crimes, were in for a different treatment, simply because they were potential terrorists. There was a possibility that they were terrorists. When making an assessment in terms of counter-intelligence work, you cannot be certain these members of that unit had committed crimes or not. They could still have been carrying weapons and were still potential perpetrators of crimes. You can't rely on the fact that when caught or captured, a person like that would stay calm and not use a hand grenade or his weapon instead. A true commander exercises command and soldiers are the ones carrying out his orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What do you mean by the phrase, "a person like that"?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: I meant the persons that you specified, who had disguised themselves and gone on to the hospital, instead of surrendering with their own battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The 18th, the Mitnica Battalion, it's right that there was or what I will call negotiations, surrender negotiations, at Mitnica which then resulted in them being taken to Ovcara; that is right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Following their surrender, they were taken to that hangar. If the hangar is at Ovcara, well, yes, in that case, they too were taken to Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, you know perfectly well that hangar is at Ovcara. Why do you play games and pretend that you don't know that?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Please, sir, I'm trying to be as specific as I possibly can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, you know perfectly well that the Mitnica Battalion was taken to Ovcara. You know that because you've been asked how many times have you been to Ovcara and you say I've only been twice on the 18th and 19th. So you know it's Ovcara. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Please, sir. When I'm talking from the point of view of a captain back in 1991, I'm telling you at the time I didn't know that the hangar was at Ovcara. If we are talking about the point in time when I gave all those statements, or indeed now, in that case, yes, we do agree. I do now know that it was at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And you went to Ovcara. You haven't told us how you got there on the 18th. How did you get there?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: I don't remember. I know somebody drove me there in a vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, who is the person who drove you?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: I don't remember. At any rate, it was someone who was aware of the setup and the hangar there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So the person who drove you, he was the person who knew where he was going; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You didn't know where you were going? For you, it was a magical mystery tour, something like that, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: No. I was supposed to go to the facility where the Mitnica Battalion had been put up, and to tell them about this suggestion concerning prevention. I personally didn't know how to drive there, how to get there in a car, so somebody who knew the way gave me a lift.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But the situation that you had was that you were to go back on the 19th, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: The next day, I went again, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. But what I'm suggesting to you is that you knew on the 18th that you would have to return on the 19th, to make sure that they were taken out of the hangar, that the Geneva Convention had been properly adhered to, and they were then dispatched, all of them, to an appropriate destination. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: The evening of the 18th, I was given the task by Mr. Sljivancanin to monitor the transport of the Mitnica Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm suggesting to you that you went to Mitnica -- that you went to Ovcara where the Mitnica Battalion was located, that you were there, not in the evening, but you were there in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Which day?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That is the 18th of November. I'm terribly sorry, I don't know what day it was.

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: We are talking about the day when the negotiations took place and the surrender of the Mitnica Battalion. Just before nightfall that day, I went to the hangar, and 20 minutes, possibly half an hour later, I drove back to Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So if I suggest to you, because we've got various diaries here with entries, if I suggest to you that here on the 18th of November, at around about 4.00, or 1600 hours in military terms, you were at the Ovcara hangar, would you agree with that as being a fair approximation?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Nightfall was at about 1630, 1700 hours, which means that it was dark by the time I reached the hangar where the Mitnica Battalion had been put up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No. I'm suggesting to you that you arrived at that hangar before it got dark. I'm not suggesting it was brilliant light, but I'm suggesting to you around about 4.00 you were at the Ovcara --

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I didn't hear your answer. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: I'm saying dusk. Yes, dusk.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Dusk an interesting concept. Would you accept the time of 4.00 or 4.30, something like that? Would that be fair?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, can we just deal then with the procedure that you had to adopt when you got there? Your task, your function, was to ensure that the Mitnica Battalion was properly treated and there should be no abuses. Would you accept that as a general proposition?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: My task was to convey the suggestion that both parties should be refrained from causing any problems that might escalate into a clash, that they should both adhere to the rules that neither side should taunt the other to ensure a smooth progress.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, the Mitnica Battalion weren't armed, the JNA soldiers were armed. While taunts may well apply, the reality is you were there to ensure that there was no malpractice or abuse of those soldiers under the JNA control. That is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Please, sir. We couldn't have been certain at the time that the Mitnica Battalion had no intention of breaking out of the hangar, of escaping, given the numerical strength on both sides. No one can be certain that given the right circumstances, the Mitnica Battalion would not have attempted to storm the hangar, take it by force, or indeed escape. That's the one thing. On the other hand, you have the behaviour of our soldiers. The third aspect of this situation is the knife that Karaula is carrying, not to mention anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, can I just set aside the knife? Can you just show us with your fingers the dimensions of the blade of the knife itself actually? Can you just hold your two fingers up and show us the knife that Karaula had?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: It was a small knife, and that's what I said. But the fact is that the security detail commander did not have this piece of information that Karaula had been allowed to keep the knife.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I've asked you just to demonstrate between your two fingers the size of this knife that he had that was such a concern?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And the blade was half that, would that be right?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: This would be the size.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And your soldiers had Kalashnikovs presumably, would that be right?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, what I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, the record might record an indication, something about ten centimetres or a little more?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm sorry. I had forgotten about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, what I would like to know is this: Would it be right to say the reason that you spoke to the officer in charge of the JNA soldiers was because he had an extremely important task, that as far as you were aware, he controlled the situation? Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: I spoke to both at the same time, the commander of the security and Mr. Karaula, at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But I am talking to you about the officer in charge of the JNA soldiers. You spoke to him because he was basically in control of the situation, in realistic terms?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: He was in charge of security.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And did you consider it to be an important task, the fact that you should ensure that everybody understood what you were saying to them about adherence to the Geneva Convention?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And I think it's right to say, and forgive me if my memory is wrong, I think you stayed ten or 15 minutes; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And when you spoke to the officers, was that inside or outside the hangar? That's Karaula and the officer of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: In front of the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And it would be right to say that that conversation was with the JNA officer principally for that period, would that be right, before you left?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: The conversation was held in the presence of both of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And the conversation lasted ten or 15 minutes?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I deal, then, please, with where did you go afterwards? I think from memory you said you went to Negoslavci. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, we have got an exhibit, the Court know it and I'm not going to refer to it unless it's absolutely necessary, but it's right, is it not, that, as you've already said, you introduced yourself so he knew who he was dealing with? Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: I introduced myself to both of them. I don't know who you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, there is one question that I'm curious about and it is this: Normally if you were dealing with a handover or in ensuring that things behave -- people behave properly, you find out the name of the person to whom you're talking to and the officer who is principally in charge, just in case you need to speak to him or somebody else needs to speak to him. Do you see my point?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: So somebody gave a task to the commander of the security, in military sense, prepared him for the -- for securing the hangar and the prisoners there. Somebody had transported those prisoners to the hangar. The prisoners entered the hangar. The moment when I appear is solely to make this suggestion, to prevent something that shouldn't happen from happening. So the only reason why I was there was this. Now, as to who actually issued the order in military terms, in combat terms, to this commander of the security detail, I don't know. I don't know who had brought, transported the prisoners there. This was simply a preventive action.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It's my fault for perhaps not indicating exactly the point accurately. I am asking or inquiring, if one is dealing with a commander in charge of the security of, as we know, I think 182 people who have surrendered, what I will call prisoners of war, one would expect to know who it is you are speaking to. For example, something might happen when you return. Someone might ask you, "Who did you speak to?" Someone might ask you, "Who is in charge there?" I'm asking, did you inquire -- did you inquire of his name to make sure that you would be covered in those areas?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: It is possible that the captain actually introduced himself, but I did not remember his name. And had there been any need for me to call him later on, or for him to call me, regarding any prisoner-related issue, there was no such need because this was not within the purview of me and of the security organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But that's not right, is it? The reality is you were there to ensure that everything was being done properly. So therefore you have to take into account all eventualities, one of those eventualities you've already mentioned to us, that this particular battalion might have turned on their soldiers. So I'd like to move off this point fairly quickly. Did he or did he not or did you inquire of his name and the unit to which he belonged?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: I don't follow. Did the commander of the security detail ask about my name or did I ask his name? I didn't understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you ask of his name?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you ask of his unit?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you say to him, "Should anything go wrong, we have to be able to contact someone"? How were you going to ensure that there was contact if there was a problem?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Please, sir. Let me repeat. He had been given his task down his chain of command from his superior. That's one thing. Secondly, there was absolutely no need for the commander to contact me regarding any issue whatsoever. This was a command task and it simply means that somebody within the chain of command ordered him to prepare his unit to take the control of the hangar, of the building, to secure it and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let us just follow, then, your path on the 18th. Within 15 minutes, you were away from Ovcara. That is right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And you say that you went to Negoslavci; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And at no time on the 18th did you return to the general area of Ovcara. That is right also, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Do you by any chance know of a place which is -- I think it's called Sremski front and Sid?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: I've already answered this question when the Defence counsel asked me. The town of Sid, the only time I visited it was in 2003, with a high-ranking political state official, on official business, and until that time, I had never been there at all, never, ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And so you knew nothing about a school in that area, or staying or being at that school on the night of the 18th; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: What school are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, we have heard evidence, you see, that you gave a forwarding place where you would be. It wasn't at Negoslavci because Negoslavci is where the security organ tend to reside. You were actually saying on that evening, we would suggest, that you were at Sid, and you told Vezmarovic that. You don't accept that; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: This is patently untrue. Please. Throughout the tour of duty of the Guards Brigade in Negoslavci, while it was stationed there, I never went to any other place, and Sid, least of all. That is so patently untrue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And is it correct that when you left the hangar at Ovcara on the 18th, that you were aware that you had to return on the 19th to ensure the continuation of the evacuation?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: No. Because I was not in charge of the evacuation. I was given this task to go back there the next morning, later on. At that time I was not quite clear what it meant actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, what do you mean, it's not quite clear. Because I'll suggest what's clear to you, that when you were there on the 18th, and spoke to Vezmarovic, you indicated to him that you would be returning, perhaps that evening, but almost certainly on the 19th?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: No, no. This is completely incorrect. I have absolutely no comment when you put such things to me. The task was given to me by Mr. Sljivancanin. It was later on, in the office, to monitor the transport, to see whether everything went well, so I couldn't have known that before Mr. Sljivancanin gave me this task.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So we get it absolutely clear, you didn't say to Vezmarovic, you would be back the next day? It was only by chance and a subsequent order by Sljivancanin that you arrived the next day? That's what you're saying, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And the reality also of the situation is that he saw you on the 19th in the morning; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: I was there in the morning, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can you just remind us again, please, while I just hunt in my notebook, I think you stayed there at Ovcara, I think you say, one and a half to two hours; is that right, on the morning of the 19th?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Approximately, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what were you doing that morning at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: The task was to go there and to verify whether everything was fine, whether the boarding was proceeding well, and whether there were any counter-intelligence-related problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So who did you ask about these topics? The same security officer?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: I think I asked him whether he had any observations to make, but not just him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But I want to try and go into a little more detail. Forgive me, I don't fully understand. You're asking about whether there was any trouble, would that be correct, through the evening, the previous evening; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: That was the usual question: Is everything fine? Not the preceding evening, but at all times during the boarding and so on. This was just the usual question one asks, is everything fine?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And the boarding, how many buses, approximately, were there?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Three, four buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And would it be right to say that the procedure for boarding was to bring them a bus to the hangar and then move individuals in in an independent way? Describe to us how it was done, please, with the assistance of the officer.

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: As far as I'm able to recall, the people who were in charge of this procedure were doing it like this: Food was distributed in front of the entrance, and then maybe some 15 metres away from there there were buses, and after people took food, they boarded the buses. That is as far as I was able to see and recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But the reason that it took one and a half to two hours was because one was bringing them out in small groups; would that be right?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: If you want to say that I was there specifically because of them, that was not the case. I did not remain there until the end there in front of the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No, but you told us you were there for one and a half hours to two hours. I just want to know what you were doing, what the procedure was when you were there.

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: From -- for my part, the procedure was non-existent. There is a method in the work of intelligence officers, which is called personal observation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And can I then perhaps shorten it then this way: That the officer who was in charge of security was around and about through that period to make sure that things were proceeding properly? Would that be a fair way of putting it?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: No, no. I was an intelligence officer. I was not a security officer. I was not in charge of the security of the Mitnica Battalion troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, what shall we call Vezmarovic? What title shall we give him? The commander of security?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Vezmarovic was the komandir of the unit that was tasked with securing the Mitnica Battalion members.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So can I put it this way, then? That through that one and a half to two hours, the komandir, i.e., Vezmarovic, was there ensuring that it was done properly? Would that be a fair way of putting it?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: I don't know how long Vezmarovic spent there, but he and his unit were tasked with securing, protecting the Mitnica Battalion and he received that task down the chain of command, I assume from his superior officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I'll approach it a different way. It's right, isn't it, that Vezmarovic remained at the Ovcara hangar for the period that you were there? Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: The hour or the one hour and a half, he was there, as far as I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It's my error and I apologise for it. I go back to the 18th. Did you see buses on the 18th, when you arrived at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When you arrived there, presumably you wanted to make sure that all of the Mitnica Battalion was under proper supervision and control, and that's why you suggested the rope. Would that be fair?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: I suggested to both sides that if they thought it necessary, they could string this piece of rope so that there would be some kind of a fence and that people would not be crossing over, to prevent any incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And that was your way to make sure that all of the Mitnica Battalion was under proper supervision; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: That was just a suggestion I made to the security commander, komandir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But it was to ensure that 182 people were kept under control; isn't that right? If Mr. Borovic could keep his voice down, I would be very grateful. That's right, isn't it? Mr. Karanfilov? It was a way of making sure that 182 people were kept under control?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: The situation would have been under control even without this measure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It's a way of ensuring that the Mitnica Battalion was kept under control; that is right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: The rope was not put -- in fact, the suggestion about the rope was not made only because of the Mitnica Battalion. It was because of both sides and this was just a suggestion that need not have been taken at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I understand exactly what you're saying, but would it be right to say, that there was, perhaps, a natural concern that you had 182 soldiers and officers under JNA supervision at that time?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Natural concern? What do you mean? In what sense?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: In the following sense: You have a battalion -- you have a battalion of people who were combatants. You have said that you spoke to Karaula and Vezmarovic to ensure that neither side would aggravate the other. Do you follow me? And therefore, if you have --

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: -- 182 people, because that's the number that -- that was the number of the Mitnica Battalion. If you had that many, you had to make sure they were kept under proper supervision. Simple point, I'd suggest.

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: The rope -- the purpose of the rope should have been, and I hope that in fact it was, to limit the movement of both sides, to restrict their -- the area where they could move. And I have to repeat: I assume that the commander of the security detail had been given very strict tasks and the manner in which this task was to be carried out, in terms of securing those prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But I repeat, since it's obviously the way I'm putting the question: There was always a danger of a battalion turning nasty and, therefore, security at that time had to be put in place to make sure that didn't occur; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BORCE KARANFILOV
utterances.text: Let's put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, would that be an appropriate moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moore. Before we break, could I indicate, Mr. Domazet, that inquiries have indicated that on Tuesday the 5th, the only change possible in the sitting would be for this Chamber to sit between 1.00 and 5.00 p.m. That is about half an hour less than we would normally sit. It would be one break of about halfway through that period. That would allow a court, an appeal which is scheduled to finish at 12.30 to finish and another proceeding, which is scheduled for 5.30 to commence. That is the only change possible on Tuesday, and unfortunately no change is possible on the Wednesday because the times have been set to allow for the arrival times of counsel who are flying in. Is that change on Tuesday something that would be convenient to all people and would the loss of about half an hour sitting time be a problem? Are there any submissions?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as far as I'm concerned, and in fact the Defence team is concerned, we would accept this possibility and I would like to thank you, because that would make it possible for me to attend the trial. In light of what Mr. Lukic said today, that he would take one session at the most for the examination-in-chief, I would need one more session for my examination. I will strife to do so, to complete it, and then this problem that I have would be solved. I think that this is something that would be to the liking of Mr. Lukic and that is definitely a solution for me. It really works for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I see no resistance and Mr. Domazet has lowered his bid for time from one and a half sessions to one session, so I think we will decide upon that now. On Tuesday then, sitting from 1.00 until 5.00. Otherwise, the times will remain during next week as programmed. We adjourn now and resume tomorrow at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
